Data and the information cutoff

What it forecasts. The German–Luxembourg day-ahead price of each hour of the next delivery day, in EUR/MWh: 24 values on most days and 23 or 25 on daylight-saving transition days, issued together as one curve before the 12:00 CET auction gate.

Where the data comes from. The committed development snapshot of the day-ahead price and the day-ahead load forecast, from SMARD.de, which republishes the ENTSO-E series, and the GFS weather forecasts, each under its registered vintage, from 2019-01-01 to 2026-09-06. Data: ENTSO-E Transparency Platform; Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de — CC BY 4.0.

The information cutoff. Each forecast uses only data published strictly before 11:00 Berlin time on the day before delivery; no price of the delivery day enters, and a training target enters only once its price was published. The live product reads the same sources every day; this report reads none of its records.

Fitting. v6 is refitted every day on the 728 days before the forecast, from network configurations that searches run every 182 days chose on earlier data only. Its development results end on 2026-09-06; 4.7T's window begins the next day.

Preprocessing. A quarter-hour series becomes an hour only from four complete quarter-hours; from 2025-10-01 the hourly price is the mean of four quarter-hour prices. The price is not log-transformed, because it is often negative.

Price regimes and negative prices

Three regimes shape the development period: before 2021-09-01, the energy crisis from 2021-09-01 to 2022-12-31, and from 2023-01-01 a market with frequent negative prices. Across v5's five test periods they hold 4,319, 2,112 and 4,316 hours; 465 of those hours, on 85 days, had a negative price.

Why it matters: the daily 728-day window holds each regime while it lasts and lets it go two years later, so the errors are reported per test period, the 2022 crisis among them, and on every development day.

v6's error in each regime, in Product results

Yearly price levels and negative-hour counts, in the archived report

The inputs it uses, and why

What it reads. DDNN-2 reads exactly v4's sources in day-level form, one row per delivery day: the price history, the day-ahead load forecast, the calendar and three regional GFS weather inputs, each as available at the issue time. It forecasts the 24 hours together, each as a full probability distribution, and issues that distribution's seven quantiles.

Why hour-of-day and day-of-week inputs. The price spectrum shows pronounced cycles at 24 and 168 hours, with a 12-hour harmonic, and their amplitude changed in the crisis; the calendar inputs follow that structure rather than assuming it.

The spectral figures behind the calendar inputs, in the archived report

How it was selected and how it will be tested

Before the test. The re-baseline issued every policy daily on every development day, 2020-12-29 to 2026-09-06, under one protocol; the selection rule, set before the re-baseline's first score, chose v6 among seven arms there in one look; and v6 was then scored on v5's five test periods. All of this is development evidence after selection. The test. 4.7T, registered before any of its 90 days' data was opened, is its one test, from 2026-12-04. Live. The live product's issued forecasts are scored after the fact, prospective evaluation in progress, and never pooled with either.

Measured results

On every development day, against v5: −7% [−9%, −5%] in point error and −11% [−13%, −9%] in interval error. On v5's five test periods: −6% [−9%, −2%] and −11% [−15%, −8%] as shares of its error scores; mean absolute error 4.5–13.4 EUR/MWh in the ordinary periods and 43.2 EUR/MWh in the 2022 crisis period. Development evidence after selection, not a test on new data.

Where it fails

Where it fails. Its largest errors are in the 2022 crisis period: a mean absolute error of 43.2 EUR/MWh, against 4.5–13.4 in the ordinary periods. On 18 development days a network member failed and the control's forecast stood in; none of them falls in the five test periods.

v6's error month by month, in Product results

Each test period, in the v6 chapter

How reliable its intervals are

How reliable its intervals are. On v5's five test periods its 95% intervals covered 0.9447 of the hours at a mean width of 82.4 EUR/MWh, narrower than v5's at similar coverage. The live product's Reliability view tracks coverage with width on the issued days; the nominal level is a reference, not a promise.

Read a forecast

Read a forecast on the live product. It shows each day's issued forecast with its nominal bands, the published prices once they exist, and the scores of the issued forecasts, labelled prospective evaluation in progress. This report shows no live forecast, score or price.

Limitations

Its limits. The results are development evidence after selection; 4.7T, from 2026-12-04, is its one test on new data. On the five test periods its information differs from v5's. The weather run's timing is fragile: a six-hour delay was measured on v5, and v6 reads the same weather inputs. The load forecast's historical values are not their original vintages, and the published prices may still be revised. A failed network member stops the day's fit, and the frozen fallback issues. It is frozen: any change needs a new freeze and a new test.

Run and check this product

Check the frozen policy. python -m cp17.tools.refreeze verify docs/track-b/evidence/cp-17c/freeze-manifest.json checks the package, its runtime and its state against the freeze and prints "verified"; the policy identity begins 720fc581. Train it yourself. The live product retrains one issued day's fit in your browser, with the same package, and says whether it matched.

What drives its forecasts

Which inputs moved v6's median on two development days: 2026-03-29, the spring clock-change day (23 hours), and 2026-09-06, the last development day. The attribution is the one committed, before the freeze, by the probe that measured its in-browser retraining: exact baseline Shapley over the input groups that day's networks use. Its fits are v6's stored forecasts for both days, quantile for quantile. On both days the load forecast for the delivery day and the weather forecast moved the median most: on average 14.0 and 14.4 EUR/MWh an hour on the first day, 43.7 and 30.8 on the second.

Drawn: the nine groups both days' networks use. Prices two days before, used on the last day only, moved the median by 2.7 EUR/MWh an hour; the holidays, day type and month group is used on neither day.

Each value attributes that day's issued median within one fitted model, relative to its networks' training-mean baseline. It is not a cause, not the value an input adds, and not how the model behaves on other days; two days are not the development period.

Business insights

The intended use. An hourly price forecast for the next delivery day, with intervals, issued before the 12:00 auction: an input to bidding, scheduling and hedging decisions in the German–Luxembourg market.

What the results imply for that use. On an average development day the median misses the hourly price by 17.2 EUR/MWh, against the naive's 34.6, and by 30.7 in the crisis; an 80% interval about 51.7 EUR/MWh wide held 0.7826 of the hours. A decision that uses the forecast can size its margin to that spread.

What is not established. No decision policy, cost model or trading simulation has been authorized or run for this product, so there is no profit, value or loss figure, and no curve of either. Lower forecast error and interval coverage are not profit, and not a success rate of any decision.

Limits. These are development results after selection; 4.7T, from 2026-12-04, is v6's one test on new data, and the live record on the Space is prospective evaluation in progress.

How the models compare

A fair comparison

The five test periods are called folds below; the third covers the 2022 price crisis. These are development results, not a test on new data.

Bootstrap settings and the five historical test periods

Paired intervals come from a moving-block bootstrap with seed 15042, 2,000 replicates and 7-day blocks, resampled identically for every policy. They are confidence intervals of an estimated difference, not forecast intervals. A change's interval as a share of the comparator's score is, from v4 on, the percentile interval of the ratio of the two scores over the same draws; for v2 and v3, it is the difference's interval divided by the comparator's score.

Definitions, the policies tested, and why v1 scores differently in its own report

The point-error score (S_MAE) is the mean over the five historical test periods (folds) of a policy's MAE divided by the similar-day naive's MAE in the same period; the interval score (S_WIS) does the same for the weighted interval score, which rewards narrow intervals and penalizes missed outcomes. MAE uses the emitted median.

The 25 policies tested against the targets, each identity counted once, by decision date. Decided 2026-09-16: Normalized LEAR; Normalized LightGBM; Normalized component mean; 84-day normalized LEAR; Normalized component mean, variant. Decided 2026-09-23: v2 · blended LEAR, hour-aware intervals; Pooled-interval control. Decided 2026-09-24: v3 · weather features. Decided 2026-09-30: v4 · three-block LightGBM added; Pooled LightGBM with weather; Three-block LightGBM; Normalized three-block LightGBM. Decided 2026-10-04: DDNN member on v4; v3 plus a capacity-averaged pooled LightGBM; v3 plus pooled normalized and raw LightGBM; v3 plus a pooled normalized LightGBM; v3 plus a pooled raw LightGBM; v3 plus normalized block LightGBM; v4 with dynamic intervals; v3 with dynamic intervals; DDNN alone; v3 plus a DDNN member. Decided 2026-10-11: v5 · DDNN-2 added; DDNN-2 alone; v3 plus a DDNN-2 member.

Why v1 scores 1.052 in the shared development comparison but 28.58% worse in its own report. Both figures describe the same 448 development days. v1's report compared its daily absolute error with the raw similar-day naive (MAE 32.45 EUR/MWh) and pooled all days, so the 2022 crisis dominates. This comparison gives each of the five folds equal weight, and its naive reference is the forecast's emitted median after the common residual layer (MAE 32.81 EUR/MWh). v1's own error is 41.74 EUR/MWh in both. v1's original nine-quantile pinball is a different score from the seven-quantile interval score used here.

Changes between generations, newest first

From v5 to v6: DDNN-2 alone

Development · post-selection

Predecessor
v5 · DDNN-2 added. In October 2026, v5 was adopted in research.
What changed
v6 keeps only v5's distributional neural network, DDNN-2, with its own quantiles, refitted every day; v5's two LEAR forecasts, its LightGBM and the blend are dropped. It is A1 in the frozen records.
Comparator
Set in advance: v5 itself, the control of the selection rule, so the comparator is the predecessor; the selection ran on every development day, and the same comparison on v5's five test periods is in v6's chapter.
Result
On every development day: −7% [−9%, −5%] in point error and −11% [−13%, −9%] in interval error, descriptive 95% intervals; on the five test periods: −6% [−9%, −2%] on the point-error score and −11% [−15%, −8%] on the interval score, as shares of v5's scores. Development, after selection; not 4.7T.
Not established
Performance on new data: 4.7T, from 2026-12-04, is its one test. Equal information with v5: its forecasts come from a later, daily protocol.
Decision
On 2026-10-25 the selection rule, set on 2026-10-12, picked arm A1, now v6, among 7 arms; the six others, blends of v5's members, also passed every gate and were not selected. It was frozen on 2026-10-28 and re-frozen on 2026-10-29 and 2026-10-30, its fit unchanged. In October 2026, v6 became the final candidate. It was selected by its own rule, never adopted by v5's. v1 is the last released generation, and the product again if 4.7T does not pass.

The comparison chart and its evidence, in the v6 chapter

From v4 to v5: adding a distributional neural network

Development · post-selection

Predecessor
v4 · three-block LightGBM added. In September 2026, v4 was adopted in research.
What changed
v5 kept v4's inputs, its two LEAR forecasts and its LightGBM, and added DDNN-2, a distributional neural network that forecasts the whole next day at once, with one sixth of the blend's weight, taken from the LightGBM's third; the hour-aware intervals were re-estimated on the new forecast's own errors.
Comparator
Set in advance: v4 itself, on identical hours, so the protocol's comparator is also the predecessor and the comparison is direct.
Result
Point-error score −2% [−3%, −2%] and interval score −2% [−3%, −2%], as a share of v4's score, with 95% confidence intervals of that ratio from the experiment's own bootstrap draws; at the rule's 97.5% decision level, [−3%, −2%] and [−3%, −2%]. Development evidence after selection, not a test on new data.
Not established
The comparison scores 448 of the 2,654 days of data up to the end of the development period, 2019-01-01 to 2026-04-07; 0 of them fall in October to December, and only 1 winter (December to February) contains any of them. It is the second decision on a distributional neural network over the same five test periods; only a one-shot test on days never used for development or selection protects against that reuse.
Decision
In October 2026, v5 was adopted in research. It met the adoption rule set before the experiment against v4; the released model, v1, did not change. The two study arms, DDNN-2 alone and v3 plus a DDNN-2 member, were built only to show where the change came from, and were never candidates for adoption.

The comparison chart and its evidence, in the v5 chapter

From v3 to v4: adding a LightGBM forecaster

Development · post-selection

Predecessor
v3 · weather features. In September 2026, v3 was adopted in research.
What changed
v4 kept v3's inputs and its two LEAR forecasts, added a LightGBM forecaster with one third of the blend's weight, and re-estimated the hour-aware intervals on the new forecast's own errors. The gain comes from the combination: on its own, no LightGBM arm showed an improvement over v3, but the blend improves both error scores, because a nonlinear model built from decision trees makes different errors from the two linear forecasts. The LightGBM's split into hour blocks is not shown to contribute.
Comparator
Set in advance: v3 itself, on identical hours, so the protocol's comparator is also the predecessor and the comparison is direct.
Result
Point-error score −5% [−6%, −4%] and interval score −5% [−6%, −4%], as a share of v3's score, with 95% confidence intervals of that ratio from the experiment's own bootstrap draws; development evidence, not a test on new data.
Not established
Separate hour-block models are not shown to help: the three-block against the pooled LightGBM shows no demonstrated joint preference. A gain over the August 2022 peak is not shown either: over those 17 days, v4's point error is higher than v3's.
Decision
In September 2026, v4 was adopted in research. It met the adoption rule set before the experiment against v3; the released model, v1, did not change. The three study arms were built only to separate the change into steps, and were never candidates for adoption.

The comparison chart and its evidence, in the v4 chapter

From v2 to v3: adding weather forecasts

Development · post-selection

Predecessor
v2 · blended LEAR, hour-aware intervals. In September 2026, v2 was adopted in research.
What changed
v3 kept v2's blend of two LEAR forecasts and its hour-aware intervals, and added three weather forecasts available before the auction: wind speed at 10 m and 100 m and solar radiation, each with a missing-data indicator.
Comparator
Set in advance: v2 itself, on identical hours, so the protocol's comparator is also the predecessor and the comparison is direct.
Result
Point-error score −12% [−16%, −9%] and interval score −14% [−17%, −11%], as a share of v2's score, with 95% confidence intervals; development evidence, not a test on new data.
Not established
The three weather inputs were tested together, so no single input's contribution is isolated; within the 2022 crisis period the point-error gain is not demonstrated on its own.
Decision
In September 2026, v3 was adopted in research. It met the joint improvement rule against v2 and both accuracy targets.

The comparison chart and its evidence, in the v3 chapter

From v1 to v2: a blended linear model with hour-aware intervals

Development · post-selection

Predecessor
v1 · released LightGBM. In September 2026, v1 was released.
What changed
After v1 failed in the 2022 crisis, v2 replaced its LightGBM quantile model and fixed-window calibration with an equal blend of two LEAR forecasts refitted every day, and intervals built from recent errors by hour of the day.
Comparator
Set in advance: daily LEAR, the strongest benchmark, not the predecessor v1; a pooled-interval control isolated the interval method.
Result
Against daily LEAR: point-error score −2% [−4%, −1%] and interval score −4% [−5%, −2%], as a share of daily LEAR's score, with 95% confidence intervals; development evidence, not a test on new data.
Against the predecessor
No paired interval for v2 against v1 exists: the protocol did not test that pair. As descriptive context on the same development hours, without an interval, the point-error scores are 1.052 for v1 and 0.644 for v2, and the interval scores 0.986 and 0.616. v1's one-shot holdout covers a different window and evidence class and is not compared.
Not established
The gain over daily LEAR is not attributed to hour-aware intervals alone, the blend and the interval layer are not separated, and against its pooled-interval control there is no demonstrated joint preference.
Decision
In September 2026, v2 was adopted in research. v3 was built on it.

Experiments not adopted between v1 and v2

  • Calibration experiment Not adopted September 2026

    Recalibration alone was not enough: the model itself had to adapt.

    Question, result and evidence

    Could recalibrating v1, without refitting it, repair its coverage in the 2022 crisis?

    Against v1, on the matched crisis window: the hours inside the 95% interval rose from 79 to 131 of 408.

    EvidenceCompare the runs in MLflowEngineering report, frozen 2026-09-16Review verdict, frozen 2026-09-16

  • Model comparison study Not adopted September 2026

    No policy met the criteria; the study informed v2's blend of two LEAR forecasts.

    Question, result and evidence

    Which forecasting approach copes best with the 2022 crisis?

    Nine policies on the same hours, none meeting the product criteria. Normalized LEAR cut crisis-window MAE to 49.9 EUR/MWh, but daily LEAR kept the better error scores: 0.658 and 0.639 against 0.672 and 0.646.

    EvidenceCompare the runs in MLflowEngineering report, frozen 2026-09-16Review verdict, frozen 2026-09-16

Experiments not adopted between v4 and v5

  • Pooled LightGBM member for v4 Not adopted October 2026

    Both candidates were decisively worse than v4 in one test period, with a 95% interval wholly above zero; the rule allowed none, so v4 was kept as it was.

    Question, result and evidence

    Can one pooled LightGBM, for all 24 hours, replace v4's three-block LightGBM member without losing accuracy against v4 itself?

    Against v4, over the five test periods together, neither candidate's 95% interval lay wholly above zero: the averaged member's paired difference is +0.0011 [−0.0031, +0.0054] in the point-error score and +0.0010 [−0.0028, +0.0049] in the interval score; the pair's −0.0013 [−0.0036, +0.0016] and −0.0008 [−0.0030, +0.0022]. In fold 4, both were decisively worse: point error +0.3 [+0.1, +0.4] and +0.2 [+0.1, +0.3] EUR/MWh, interval score +0.2 [+0.1, +0.2] and +0.1 [+0.024, +0.2] EUR/MWh. Development evidence after selection, not a test on new data.

    EvidenceCompare the runs in MLflowEngineering report, frozen 2026-10-04Review verdict, frozen 2026-10-04

  • DDNN member on v4 Not adopted October 2026

    Question, result and evidence

    Does a distributional neural network, added to v4 as a one-third member, improve on v4 in point and interval accuracy together?

    Against v4, the paired difference is +0.0064 [−0.0016, +0.0149] in the point-error score and +0.0071 [−0.0009, +0.0138] in the interval score, with 95% intervals; in fold 3, the 2022 crisis, its point error was decisively worse, +1.9 [+0.3, +4.4] EUR/MWh. v6 · DDNN-2 alone

DDNN-2 alone, refitted daily, frozen for 4.7T; A1 in the frozen records

Development · post-selection

What this result does not establish

  • That the two had the same information. v6's forecasts were made under the later daily protocol: issued one or two hours earlier, refitted every day, with its own network searches and data identity. Its forecasts cover the first period, 2020, though that protocol's scores began after it. Under v5's protocol, v5's study arm of the same name scored 0.4785 and 0.4271 on these hours. The comparison shares the hours and prices, not the protocol.
  • Performance on new data. v6 was selected on every development day, four of these periods among them, after DDNN-2 alone had already scored best there. This is development evidence after selection; 4.7T, on 90 days whose data was opened only after its registration, is its one test.

Decision

On 2026-10-25 the selection rule, set on 2026-10-12, picked arm A1, now v6, among 7 arms; the six others, blends of v5's members, also passed every gate and were not selected. It was frozen on 2026-10-28 and re-frozen on 2026-10-29 and 2026-10-30, its fit unchanged. In October 2026, v6 became the final candidate. It was selected by its own rule, never adopted by v5's. v1 is the last released generation, and the product again if 4.7T does not pass.

Method

The model. DDNN-2 is a feed-forward network written in NumPy that forecasts the 24 hours of a day at once, each as a full probability distribution; v6 issues that distribution's own seven quantiles. Eight networks, the four best configurations of its last search with two seeds each, are fitted every day and combined.

The scoring. v6's stored forecasts cover 10,747 of the 10,747 hours. They were scored by v5's own scoring code, against the same observed prices, with the same bootstrap draws; the recomputed scores of v5 and the naive equal their published values exactly.

How v6's forecasts differ from v5's in these periods

Where the two protocols differ in these periods. Issue time: 11:00 Berlin for v6, 11:00 UTC for v5. Fitting: daily refits on the last 728 days for v6, one fit per test period for v5. Search: v6's networks come from searches run every 182 days on earlier data only. Data: a later data identity and registered input vintages. The first period: in v6's protocol it falls in an unscored warm-up, with less than 728 days of history.

The stress period: the 2022 crisis

The 2022 crisis period

In the 2022 crisis period, the third test period, v6's mean absolute error was 43.2 EUR/MWh against v5's 45.5; the paired difference in mean daily error is −2.31 [−5.04, +1.51] EUR/MWh, with its 95% interval.

Coverage and interval width

Interval coverage and width

Pooled over the five periods, v6's 95% intervals covered 0.9447 of the hours at a mean width of 82.4 EUR/MWh; v5's covered 0.9395 at 100.2 EUR/MWh. Narrower intervals with similar coverage; the nominal 95% is a reference, not a target.

Protocol and review

How v6 was selected

The selection rule, set on 2026-10-12 and frozen before the re-baseline's first score: seven recombinations of v5's members, v6 among them, each against v5 on every development day. To pass, an arm had to beat v5 by more than half a percent on both scores, lose no more than 2% in any complete year from 2021 to 2025 or any season, and survive Holm's correction across the seven at 5%, in the main analysis and in three sensitivity variants. Among those that passed, the lowest interval error won.

All seven passed every analysis. v6 had the lowest interval error, 9.68 EUR/MWh against the next best's 10.13, so it was selected; its largest p-value in the main analysis was 0.0042. The table gives every arm's change against v5, with descriptive 95% intervals.

The selection was run only after the Owner saw the re-baseline's report, which already showed DDNN-2 alone on these days; its multiplicity control is conditional on that decision.

The freeze

The freeze. On 2026-10-28 v6 was frozen as the product's complete daily policy: one package, run unchanged by the issuing host and by the visitor's browser. It was re-frozen on 2026-10-29 with the Owner's later decisions, and on 2026-10-30 under the issuing host, Pyodide in Node.js on a macOS runner or the Owner's Mac, where all 58 fits came out identical bit for bit. Its policy identity begins 720fc581; any change to the policy, its code, runtime or state needs a new freeze and a new test.

4.7T, registered before the test

4.7T, registered before the test. One test of v6, on delivery days 2026-09-07 to 2026-12-05, 90 days, opening no earlier than 2026-12-04, once every price is published. The window is never extended, shortened or rolled.

Against what, and how. The control is v5, the reference the similar-day naive, both run under the re-baseline's rules; v3, v4 and v1's released model are reported, never tested. The scores are each day's mean absolute error of the median and its interval score. It passes when the largest of four one-sided p-values is at most 0.05: v6 better than v5 by more than half a percent on both scores, and better than the naive on both. The p-values come from a 7-day block bootstrap with 10,000 draws.

The failure rules. At least 60 of the 90 days must be paired and scored, or the test is inconclusive. No runner-up moves up, the window is spent whatever the result, and a null result is valid.

What each result means. A pass keeps v6 as the product and ends its "pending" status; the record says "It passed the pre-registered test". A fail or an inconclusive result makes v1 the product again, and the record says "It did not pass; the window is spent, and v1 remains the product." While v6 runs on the Space, its live record stays "prospective evaluation in progress" until at least 90 consecutive days are scored.

v5 · DDNN-2 added

v4 plus a DDNN-2 member

Development · post-selection

What this result does not establish

  • That the gain holds across the year. The comparison scores 448 of the 2,654 days of data up to the end of the development period, 2019-01-01 to 2026-04-07; 0 of them fall in October to December, and only 1 winter (December to February) contains any of them.
  • Performance on new data. This is development evidence after selection, and the second decision on a distributional neural network over the same five test periods, after the DDNN member on v4; only a one-shot test on days never used for development or selection protects against that reuse.
  • That DDNN-2 is best used as v5 uses it. DDNN-2 alone had lower, that is better, error scores than v4: −11% [−14%, −7%] on the point-error score and −16% [−19%, −12%] on the interval score, as shares of v4's score, with 95% confidence intervals; v3 plus a DDNN-2 member also scored better than v5. Descriptive only: both were study arms, never eligible for adoption, and no rule tested them.

Decision

In October 2026, v5 was adopted in research. It met the adoption rule set before the experiment against v4; the released model, v1, did not change. The two study arms, DDNN-2 alone and v3 plus a DDNN-2 member, were built only to show where the change came from, and were never candidates for adoption.

Method

The blend. v5's central forecast gives v4's two LEAR forecasts, bit for bit, two thirds of the weight, v4's LightGBM one sixth and DDNN-2 one sixth. The weights were fixed before any fit and never tuned. The hour-aware intervals keep v4's recipe, re-estimated on v5's own errors.

DDNN-2. A feed-forward network written in NumPy, on one row per delivery day, with a Johnson SU distribution for each of the 24 hours, and exactly v4's information. Each member trains on up to two years before the forecast day, from 2019-01-01 at the earliest, minus a random fifth of whole weeks held out to stop its training; four configurations, chosen per test period by a search on training data only, times two seeds, are combined by the median of their forecasts.

The study arms: DDNN-2 alone, and DDNN-2 in the LightGBM's place

The study arms. DDNN-2 alone, against v4: −11% [−14%, −7%] on the point-error score and −16% [−19%, −12%] on the interval score, as shares of v4's score: descriptive, never eligible.

v3 plus a DDNN-2 member, DDNN-2 in the LightGBM's place, scored better than v5 itself: v5 minus it is +0.0067 [+0.0033, +0.0097] on the point-error score and +0.0062 [+0.0031, +0.0089] on the interval score, both intervals wholly above zero: with DDNN-2 present, adding the LightGBM member made both scores worse. It too was a study arm, never eligible, so the rule's candidate was v5.

Coverage and interval width

Did the intervals get more reliable, or only wider?

v5's pooled intervals are narrower than v4's at every level: mean widths 25.3, 54.7 and 100.2 EUR/MWh at the 50%, 80% and 95% levels, against 26.3, 56.1 and 101.9. Its pooled coverage is 0.4916, 0.7923 and 0.9395, against v4's 0.4961, 0.7905 and 0.9392.

Protocol and review

The rule, set on 2026-10-05 and frozen in the protocol before any of its fits: v5 would be adopted only if, against v4, the paired differences' intervals at 97.5% lay below zero for the interval score and at or below zero for the point-error score; it met the six original screening criteria; the evaluation was complete and valid; no test period was decisively worse, that is, none had a 95% paired interval wholly above zero; and both point estimates improved on v4's score by at least half a percent. The 97.5% level splits a 5% error rate across the two attempts the plan allowed; one ran. All five conditions held.

As a diagnostic, v5 meets all six original screening criteria, as v4, DDNN-2 alone and v3 plus a DDNN-2 member do. This is a development diagnostic, not a product qualification.

All 80 frozen causal and integrity controls passed, each negative check paired with a positive one: masking the delivery day and future inputs changed the forecast by exactly zero, and a day-before price change, weather permutations and held-out weeks moved DDNN-2.

No delivery-day outcome is used: the leakage test at every origin

No outcome from the delivery day on is used, at any origin. With every such outcome destroyed, the frozen network refitted at all 636 warm-up and evaluation origins reproduced the committed forecasts bit for bit at 636 of them, over 10,747 hours; a change to the previous day's prices moved them, and a planted one-day leak was caught in every test period. The input vintages are inherited from the earlier experiments, not re-tested here.

Method

The blend. v4's central forecast gives v3's two LEAR forecasts, bit for bit, two thirds of the weight, and the mean of the raw and normalized three-block LightGBM forecasts one third. The weights were fixed before any result and never tuned. The hour-aware intervals keep v3's recipe, re-estimated on v4's own errors.

The same information as v3. Every LightGBM arm uses the model comparison study's LightGBM inputs plus the three weather forecasts and their missing-data indicators. The blocks are the night, the solar hours and the shoulder and peak hours, in local time. At every forecast origin each block picks one of 4 model sizes on the training window's last 28 days, by MAE, then refits.

The ladder. Three study arms separate the change into steps, one at a time. Daily LightGBM to the pooled LightGBM adds weather, bundled with the training-only choice of model size and the missing-input rule, so that step is not a weather effect on its own. The pooled to the three-block LightGBM adds the block split alone: the same rows, target, inputs, size grid, selection rule and interval recipe. v4 then blends the block models into v3.

Protocol and review

The rule, set on 2026-09-29 and frozen in the protocol before any fit: v4 would be adopted only if, against v3, the interval score's paired difference had its upper 95% confidence limit below zero and the point-error score's at or below zero; it met the six original screening criteria; the evaluation was complete and valid; and no test period was decisively worse, that is, none had a paired interval wholly above zero. All four held.

As a diagnostic, v4 meets all six original screening criteria, as v3 does. Among the study arms, the normalized three-block LightGBM meets them; the pooled LightGBM misses criterion 4 (the August 2022 peak against the benchmarks), and the three-block LightGBM misses criteria 4 and 5 (each test period against the daily benchmarks). This is a development diagnostic, not a product qualification.

Run through this experiment's code, v3 reproduced its accepted forecasts bit for bit on all 10,747 hours, so the comparison is with v3 itself.

All 49 frozen causal and integrity controls passed: masking the delivery day or future weather changed the forecast by exactly zero, a day-before price change moved every arm, and the pooled and block arms saw the same rows.

22,260 LightGBM fits in the main run. The time of one daily cycle was measured as a diagnostic, not as a qualification for daily operation.

Method

Operational NCEP GFS 0.25°, the 00 UTC run of the day before delivery. Wind components are interpolated to each delivery hour; wind speed is computed per grid cell before a cos(latitude)-weighted average over the fixed box 47–55.25°N, 5.5–15.5°E; radiation is de-averaged from the forecast's running means. Each feature has a missing indicator. A regional weather proxy: not the DE-LU zone's exact outline and not a generation forecast.

Only delivery 2019-01-01 has no weather, structurally: its run would be 2018-12-31, before the input floor. Nothing was imputed from a failed retrieval.

Availability of each run before the D−1 11:00 UTC forecast origin is reconstructed from dated NCEP production records with an assumed dissemination lag. It is not a per-day delivery guarantee.

The dashed line marks 95% of the window's hours, the nominal target: a computed reference, not an observed count; there is no coverage guarantee.

Protocol and review

As a diagnostic, v3 is the first policy evaluated against the original criteria to meet all six; v2 misses criteria 1 and 2. This is a development diagnostic, not a product qualification.

Frozen causal controls ran on 2020-07-01 and 2025-05-01: masking the delivery day or the future changed the forecast by exactly zero, an available day-before price change moved it, and future weather changed nothing.

One frozen check could not fail: multiplying all weather by a constant is undone by the training-only scaler. It was kept as an invariance check, and two controls that can fail were added, a shift of the target day's weather and a permutation of the training weather. Both passed (repair r13).

The first independent Integration review within this project's process failed: one frozen input's recorded hash described its bytes with Windows line endings, so the reproduction commands refused to run in a clean checkout. The bytes were restored to the recorded identity (repair r14) and a fresh Integration review passed.

2,476 GFS runs and 123,800 decoded messages; 136.0 GiB transferred; 40.09 machine-hours; external cost $0.

v3 needs one GFS retrieval per delivery day.

The v3 research model's weather data is derived from NCEP GFS 0.25° (NOAA/NWS/NCEP) via NCAR GDEX d084001 (doi:10.5065/D65D8PWK) and NOAA Open Data Dissemination on AWS, modified and aggregated by this project; it is not an official NOAA product.

v1 · released LightGBM

Nine-quantile LightGBM with calibrated intervals

A LightGBM ensemble forecasting nine quantiles for every hour, calibrated into 50 / 80 / 95% prediction intervals, and shipped exactly as it was evaluated.

The one-shot holdout Confirmatory-style, not power-qualified

On its pre-specified 90-day holdout, v1 beat the similar-day naive: MAE 25.9 against 27.8 EUR/MWh, and mean pinball loss 6.7 against 13.9 EUR/MWh. A one-sided Diebold–Mariano test on the daily pinball-loss vectors gave p < 10⁻⁶; it tests the probabilistic forecast, not the MAE difference.

Pre-specified one-shot holdout DM test on a fixed 90-day window — confirmatory-style, not power-qualified.

Where it falls short. On the development folds its point error is 28.58% worse than the naive's, pooled over all days (a one-sided test for an improvement gives p = 0.948: no evidence of an advantage). Over the August 2022 peak weeks its 95% interval covered 0.194 of outcomes.

Why: its crisis errors were about price level, not shape. On the crisis window the bias was −269.4 EUR/MWh, and the daily mean-level error was 269.4 EUR/MWh against a within-day shape error of 66.9 EUR/MWh.

DE-LU day-ahead price forecasting

A probabilistic forecast of the next delivery day's hourly German–Luxembourg day-ahead electricity price, with calibrated 50 / 80 / 95 % prediction intervals. Strict-gate by construction: the shipped model uses no input published after the 12:00 CET day-ahead auction gate. Evaluated exactly once, on a holdout pinned before development.

The shipped model is exactly the model the holdout evaluated: there is no retrain and no re-tune after the result was opened.

This page is static. It renders from files committed in the repository and makes no runtime call to any external service — no analytics, no fonts, no CDN, no call to the interactive Space. Everything below, including the chart, works with the network off.

1 · The data

One committed Parquet snapshot: 67,343 continuous UTC-indexed hourly rows, delivery 2019-01-01 through 2026-09-06, carrying the day-ahead price (A44), the day-ahead load forecast (A65/A01), the benchmark-only day-ahead VRE forecast (A69) and aggregate actual generation (A75). Quarter-hourly feeds aggregate to hours from exactly four complete bins, never a partial one; the 2025-10-01 switch to a 15-minute price product is handled as the mean of four quarter-hour prices. The snapshot is pinned by SHA-256 7dd2dc73407706ca6bd3c1ad51d201ac0de35eec5ca129ce320cca639f697f00 and ships inside the container, so the demo never pulls a feed while you use it.

Data: ENTSO-E Transparency Platform; Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de — CC BY 4.0.

2 · Three regimes in one series

The annual mean price swept from about €30/MWh in 2020 to about €235/MWh in 2022 and back to about €89/MWh in 2025 — a crisis and a normalization inside one training set. Underneath it, the solar build-out pushed negative-price hours from 139 (2021) → 69 (2022) → 301 (2023) → 457 (2024) → 576 (2025).

The 2025 count is measured on this snapshot's hourly series. From 2025-10-01 an hour is the mean of four quarter-hour prices, so any hour-level tally depends on that averaging choice and a quarter-hour tally differs. The price is routinely negative and has touched the −500 €/MWh floor, which is why no log or Box-Cox transform is applied to the target: pinball loss, the CQR score and monotone rearrangement are all location-equivariant and behave correctly through zero.

Two consequences the whole design follows from. Evaluation is stratified across all three regimes rather than collapsed into a recent tail. And exchangeability — the assumption CQR's coverage guarantee rests on — is mildly violated by construction, which is disclosed rather than assumed away.

3 · Feature catalog — frozen before fitting

Two catalogs were frozen before any model ran. base: calendar and regime features, the A65 load forecast, calendar-day-matched price lags at D−1 / D−2 / D−7, and D-1-frozen rolling price statistics. base + residual_load_proxy adds exactly one domain feature — a residual-load proxy built from a 42-complete-delivery-day trailing mean of actual wind and solar generation ending at D−2, which clears the 12:00 gate with a wide margin.

Pooled observation-weighted raw-head mean pinball loss over the five pinned development folds, matched on rows, seed, hyperparameters and (zero) tuning budget, unrounded as stored:

ArmPooled raw-head mean pinball loss
base13.015841509664993
base + residual_load_proxy13.064197422052183

Percentage difference (augmented vs base): +0.371516%. Selected catalog: base. The rule was fixed before fitting — the augmented catalog ships only if its unrounded stored pooled loss is lower. It is not, so the domain feature did not earn its place and the champion ships strict-gate. That is a reportable result, not a failure, and the comparison was designed so that "no improvement" was a publishable answer.

3b · Why these seasonal features? (spectral view)

The Welch periodogram shows pronounced price energy at the 24-hour and 168-hour cycles with a visible 12-hour harmonic, which is what justifies the catalog's hour-of-day and day-of-week structure rather than an assumption that electricity "should" be daily-seasonal. The per-regime overlay shows an elevated broadband floor and altered seasonal amplitude during the crisis: the spectrum itself is not stationary across regimes, which supports reporting performance across all three rather than collapsing them into one recent-tail summary. The ACF cross-check confirms the same daily and weekly recurrence in the time domain, so the conclusion does not rest on a single estimator. These are price diagnostics only — they neither validate nor justify retaining residual_load_proxy, which the frozen two-arm comparison alone decides.

4 · Validation design

Expanding-window walk-forward CV with five development folds, each carrying a one-complete-delivery-day embargo — 23, 24 or 25 rows as DST requires, never hard-coded to 24 — and a 90-day evaluation block, anchored so the blocks span pre-crisis, the crisis peak and the post-crisis negative-price era. Five tail partitions were pinned before any EDA: fold 5, Embargo A, a 60-day final-calibration slice, Embargo B, and the final 90-day holdout.

The target is D+1, anchored at the 12:00 CET gate, because that is what the day-ahead auction clears. That makes the availability rule stricter than it first looks: the model emits the whole next-day curve at once, so a row-wise t−1 boundary would admit the target curve into its own features. The binding rule is per delivery day — for a forecast of day D, every price-derived feature may consume only prices whose delivery date is earlier than D, rolling statistics are frozen at the D−1 boundary for the whole curve, and an unavailable or ambiguous calendar-day match fails closed to null rather than reaching for a same-day price.

Strict gate. The day-ahead wind and solar forecast (A69) is not published until after the 12:00 gate, so rather than use it as-archived and disclose that, this project excludes it from the shipped model entirely. Delivery-day A69 is rejected by the champion's runtime schema. What the exclusion costs is then measured, in section 5, instead of being waved at.

Two disclosed assumptions, stated as assumptions rather than as measurements:

  • A65/A01 is pre-gate by explicit assumption, not by measurement: both the existence of the delivery-day load forecast before the 12:00 CET gate and its equality to the archived vector used here are assumed, and the regulatory update provision permits later revisions.
  • A75 aggregate actual generation is used at its current archived values, which may differ from the values visible in real time despite the D-2 boundary.

5 · Results

Development folds — descriptive post-selection evidence

evidence_class = development_post_selection. These folds were also used for catalog selection and model development, so their p-values are descriptive, never confirmatory, and no result gates anything.

AnalysisComparatorStatisticp-valueN days
Probabilistic daily-vector pinballsimilar-day naive-2.55170.00536448
Point median absolute errorsimilar-day naive1.62280.948448

The point-accuracy test does not merely fail to show an advantage — it shows a deficit. The test is one-sided (reject if DM < −1.645) and the statistic is +1.6228, p = 0.948: the champion's median is 28.58% worse against the naive over the development folds. Reported here rather than omitted or reframed. The probabilistic win is broad and the point-accuracy win is not: the pooled MAE gap comes almost entirely from the crisis-peak fold. The mechanism is measured, not assumed: the model did see the crisis (that fold's training included 5,784 crisis hours at a €173 mean and a €700 maximum), but 61.3% of the evaluation block sits above the 99th percentile of everything it ever saw while only 2.45% exceeds its maximum — shrinkage toward the training level, not an extrapolation wall. Persistence has no training distribution and carries the level for free. Note also that a point forecast scored on pinball is structurally disadvantaged against a nine-quantile model, so the pinball margin is largely the value of having a predictive distribution.

The one-shot holdout — opened exactly once

After the catalog, hyperparameters and every implementation choice were frozen, the nine raw heads were fit on every eligible row strictly before Embargo A, the four CQR thresholds were estimated once on the 60-day calibration slice, isotonic-last was attached, and that complete artifact was frozen. Only then was the holdout opened.

MetricChampionSimilar-day naiveDifference
MAE (EUR/MWh)25.907827.7578-6.66%
Mean pinball loss6.708313.8789-51.67%

Final empirical coverage over 2,160 rows on 90 delivery days: 0.4407 / 0.7593 / 0.9398 at the 50 / 80 / 95 % nominal levels. Probabilistic daily-vector Diebold–Mariano against the similar-day naive: statistic -8.6798, p-value 1.98e-18, standardized effect size -1.0478.

Pre-specified one-shot holdout DM test on a fixed 90-day window — confirmatory-style, not power-qualified.

The result supports a probabilistic-skill claim against the similar-day naive on this window and nothing wider. It is not a gate, and no superiority claim beyond what it supports is made anywhere on this page.

What the post-gate forecast would have been worth

A controlled ablation on raw quantile heads, neither arm calibrated, identical in every respect except the added delivery-day A69 forecast and its named derivatives: pooled mean pinball loss moves from 13.015841509664993 to 10.478714632475889 — -19.4926%. So the project ships an honest model and puts a number on the value of the information it chose not to use.

This uncalibrated raw-head comparison isolates the information content of post-gate A69. It makes no claim about calibrated interval quality and does not make A69 available at the forecast gate.

SHAP on the p50 head explains central tendency, not interval width — width is driven by the inter-quantile spread and the CQR shift. The two rankings agree at the top and disagree in the middle, which is the ordinary difference between attribution in expectation and degradation under shuffling.

9 · Reliability — three stages

stagenominalempirical
raw LightGBM0.50.2257
raw LightGBM0.80.4322
raw LightGBM0.950.6705
post-CQR / pre-isotonic0.50.3642
post-CQR / pre-isotonic0.80.628
post-CQR / pre-isotonic0.950.8416
final post-isotonic0.50.3645
final post-isotonic0.80.6281
final post-isotonic0.950.8452

The finite-sample, distribution-free per-interval marginal guarantee attaches to the post-CQR / pre-isotonic output only. Isotonic is a monotone rearrangement applied last; whenever it moves an endpoint it perturbs the interval, so the final output's coverage is reported as empirical. No joint or simultaneous coverage across the four intervals is claimed.

The one retained hard gate is a correctness property, not a favourable number: zero quantile-crossing violations after the full pipeline. On the selected base catalog's development evaluation rows, the raw heads cross on 10,158 adjacent pairs and still cross on 4,412 after CQR; after isotonic the count is 0, and 0 on the holdout. That CQR alone leaves thousands of crossings is exactly why isotonic is unconditionally last.

CQR provides finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees under exchangeability. The walk-forward CV mildly violates exchangeability — the crisis regime is not exchangeable with the pre-crisis regime, and the solar-driven negative-price era is not exchangeable with either — so empirical coverage may diverge from nominal on regime-shift folds. This is documented in the reliability diagram (Section 8.4).

Historical out-of-sample replay — the frozen champion forecasting a 90-day period it never trained on. This is not a live forecast. Nominal level selected above; the frozen champion's own empirical coverage at that level over the 90-day holdout was 0.7593.

Scenario perturbations are ceteris-paribus sensitivity probes and may be out of distribution. The scenario holds every other input fixed, including the price history the lags and rolling statistics are built from, so a large perturbation asks the model a question it was never trained on. The cleared-price line is hidden while a scenario is active, because the outcome belongs to the unperturbed day.

11 · Honest limitations

  • Exchangeability under regime shift. CQR provides finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees under exchangeability. The walk-forward CV mildly violates exchangeability — the crisis regime is not exchangeable with the pre-crisis regime, and the solar-driven negative-price era is not exchangeable with either — so empirical coverage may diverge from nominal on regime-shift folds. This is documented in the reliability diagram (Section 8.4).
  • Development versus one-shot evidence. The five-fold development results are descriptive post-selection evidence, never confirmatory: those folds also chose the catalog. Only the 90-day holdout was pre-specified and opened once, and on the development folds the point-accuracy DM shows a deficit, not merely the absence of an advantage.
  • Disclosed assumption — the load forecast. A65/A01 is pre-gate by explicit assumption, not by measurement: both the existence of the delivery-day load forecast before the 12:00 CET gate and its equality to the archived vector used here are assumed, and the regulatory update provision permits later revisions.
  • Disclosed assumption — the generation archive. A75 aggregate actual generation is used at its current archived values, which may differ from the values visible in real time despite the D-2 boundary.
  • The measured cost of the strict gate. The strict-gate design has a measured cost rather than an assumed one: the post-gate A69 forecast is worth 19.4926% of pooled raw-head pinball loss, and the project declines to use it.
  • A two-sided bounded target, live at the floor. The target is two-sided and bounded: the price is routinely negative and has hit the −500 EUR/MWh floor, which truncates the lower conformity residuals, so the lowest intervals under-cover conditionally near the floor.
  • Coverage divergence. Empirical coverage diverges from nominal: 0.4407 / 0.7593 / 0.9398 against 50 / 80 / 95 %, so the 50 % interval under-covers by roughly six points on the holdout window. On the crisis stratum it does not merely diverge, it collapses: over the August-2022 peak weeks the 95 % interval covered 0.194 of outcomes. The mechanism is measured — that fold's CQR thresholds were estimated on a May-June 2022 calibration window at a ~198 EUR/MWh level and applied to an evaluation block averaging 376 EUR/MWh, and the conformal correction is additive, not multiplicative. This is what a split-conformal guarantee does when exchangeability breaks; it is the defect later generations address (see the v2 and v3 chapters), and it is not fixed in the released v1.
  • Model staleness, with all four cutoffs. The deployed demo applies a frozen model whose raw-model fit cutoff (2026-04-07) precedes the snapshot cutoff (2026-09-06) by 152 delivery days, with the final calibration window 2026-04-09..2026-06-07 and the holdout window 2026-06-09..2026-09-06 — all four cutoffs published separately because they are four different dates.
  • The 15-minute MTU averaging choice. From 2025-10-01 an hourly price is the mean of four quarter-hour prices, so every hour-level statistic here — the negative-hour tally included — depends on that averaging choice, and a quarter-hour tally differs.
  • Scope. This is a portfolio artifact, not an operations system: no retraining schedule, no drift gate, no rollback machinery, no monitoring surface, and no multi-day-ahead forecast.

The day-ahead price floor moved to −600 EUR/MWh from 2026-05-28, an environment shift the frozen model predates.

The holdout is a single contiguous recent period, so it tests generalization to the most recent regime rather than repeated out-of-sample skill. Its partitions were pinned before development and it was evaluated once, after the complete model and calibration pipeline were frozen, with no subsequent tuning. The 90-day length was fixed by partition design, not by a power calculation, so the Diebold–Mariano result is confirmatory-style but not power-qualified. The model shown is exactly the model evaluated — no refit followed the holdout — so its raw-model fit cutoff precedes the snapshot cutoff by 152 delivery days. Sequential lag features may use earlier holdout observations exactly as they would in live forecasting; no holdout outcome entered fitting or a development decision. Enforcement is procedural: this is a solo build and the discipline is disclosed, not cryptographically guaranteed.

The pickle's bytes are deliberately not the identity to check: MLflow stamps a fresh UUID and creation time into MLmodel on every save and cloudpickle is not byte-reproducible, so models/champion/ changes while the model does not. The fingerprint is computed over the catalog, the feature list, the nine quantiles, the four thresholds and the nine boosters' own serializations.

  • Tagged commit. Check out the tagged commit and run uv sync then make train: the champion is rebuilt from the committed snapshot with pinned dependencies and fixed seeds, no extra fetch.
  • MLflow permalinks. Every decision-bearing run — the three baselines, both catalog candidates, both benchmark arms, the champion's final fit and holdout, and the diagnostics — is public at https://dagshub.com/hrsi56/delu-day-ahead-forecast.mlflow with snapshot hash, code SHA, fold spec, feature list, seed, hyperparameters, metrics and artifact links. Counting runs there will not give you 'one', and it is not meant to: the tracking server shows several runs named champion::final-fit-and-holdout, because the script is deterministic and was re-run while CP-2 was authored — once aborted on the runtime firewall before any outcome was read, and every completed run reproducing the previous run's metrics and artifact fingerprint exactly. “Evaluated exactly once” is a statement about the evaluation decision, not about how many times a deterministic script may be executed — an Integration Critic re-running it from a clean worktree is reproducing the result, not taking a second look at the holdout. No catalog, hyperparameter, threshold or analysis choice was changed after any of them.
  • The registered champion alias. The champion is registered on that MLflow instance as the model delu-day-ahead-champion under the champion alias, carrying release and lineage tags — release_status=portfolio_release, the source run id, the code commit, the snapshot hash and the four cutoffs. It is portfolio evidence only: the deployed demo loads the bundled artifact and never queries the registry.
  • Canonical entry point. The static GitHub Pages report at https://hrsi56.github.io/delu-day-ahead-forecast/ is the canonical entry point, and the interactive Space at https://huggingface.co/spaces/Yarden-Viktor/delu-day-ahead-forecast is linked from it.
  • DuckDB SQL. The hand-authored DuckDB queries in sql/feature_queries.sql express the same calendar-day lag and D-1-frozen rolling semantics as the canonical Python pipeline, and run against the committed Parquet with make sql.
  • The four cutoffs. All four cutoffs are published separately: snapshot 2026-09-06, raw-model fit 2026-04-07, final calibration 2026-04-09..2026-06-07, holdout 2026-06-09..2026-09-06.
  • Attribution. Data: ENTSO-E Transparency Platform; Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de — CC BY 4.0. Code MIT; the redistributed data stays CC BY 4.0 with attribution, and the trained champion is a derived work of it. The v3 research model's weather data is derived from NCEP GFS 0.25° (NOAA/NWS/NCEP) via NCAR GDEX d084001 (doi:10.5065/D65D8PWK) and NOAA Open Data Dissemination on AWS, modified and aggregated by this project; it is not an official NOAA product. See LICENSE and DATA-LICENSE.md.
  • Run it yourself. Clone https://github.com/hrsi56/delu-day-ahead-forecast, then uv sync, then uv run python predict_next_day.py --level 80 --self-check forecasts a delivery day offline from the bundled snapshot and re-proves the gate boundary as it goes; make test runs the invariant suite including the CQR order-statistic fixture; make sql runs the DuckDB queries; and docker build -t delu-showcase . && docker run -p 7860:7860 delu-showcase builds and serves the same image the Space runs, champion and snapshot bundled inside it.
  • Compute. Apple M3, 16 GB, CPU only, no GPU, $0 run rate; the whole pipeline — development, benchmark, final fit and diagnostics — runs in well under an hour.

How the system works, and how to check it

How the system works

  1. Source data and vintagesENTSO-E and SMARD prices and load forecasts; from v3, the GFS run of the day before
  2. Information cutoffForecast-cutoff checks; source-availability assumptions documented
  3. FeaturesCalendar, price lags, load forecast; weather from v3
  4. Model and interval policyv1: LightGBM quantiles, conformal calibration; v2 and v3: blended LEAR, hour-aware intervals; v4: that blend plus a three-block LightGBM; v5: v4 plus a distributional neural network written in NumPy; v6, the final candidate: that network alone, refitted daily and frozen
  5. Evaluation and artifactsFive historical periods, identical hours; committed predictions, metrics and reviews
  6. Report, product and trackingThis page, the live product and v1's historical demo on the Space, and the MLflow mirror
  7. Live operationThe frozen v6 issues each day's forecast before the auction; outcomes are scored after the fact, prospective evaluation in progress

Built with Python, entsoe-py, pandas, NumPy, DuckDB, LightGBM, scikit-learn, Parquet, GitHub Actions, GitHub Pages, marimo, Pyodide, Hugging Face Static Space and MLflow on DagsHub.

Checked in code: controls that fail when a feature crosses the forecast cutoff. Assumed and documented: each source's historical availability (the availability assumptions). Dashed outlines mark planned parts.
